title: Calprotectin
desc: Calprotectin is an abundant neutrophil protein complex (an S100A8/S100A9 heterodimer) that helps defend the host by sequestering manganese and zinc from microbes, and is measured in stool as a biomarker of gut inflammation.

title: Dissimilatory Metal Reduction
desc: Dissimilatory metal reduction is a form of anaerobic microbial respiration in which cells conserve energy by transferring respiratory electrons onto an oxidized metal, such as Fe(III), Mn(IV), or U(VI), used as the terminal electron acceptor.

title: Irving–Williams Series
desc: The Irving–Williams series is the empirical order of thermodynamic stability for high-spin divalent first-row transition-metal complexes, Mn(II) < Fe(II) < Co(II) < Ni(II) < Cu(II) > Zn(II), which holds regardless of the ligand.

title: Metal Intoxication
desc: Metal intoxication is the offensive arm of nutritional immunity in which host immune cells flood a trapped microbe with toxic excess copper and zinc to mismetalate its enzymes and destroy iron-sulfur clusters.

title: Metal Sparing
desc: Metal sparing is the remodeling of a microbe's proteome during metal starvation, in which metal-requiring proteins are replaced by isozymes that use a different metal or no metal at all, thereby reducing cellular demand for the scarce element.

title: Metallochaperone
desc: A metallochaperone is a soluble intracellular carrier protein that binds a specific metal ion and delivers it by direct protein-protein contact to a designated target enzyme or transporter.

title: Metallome
desc: The metallome is the entirety of metal and metalloid species within a cell or organism, comprising free ions together with all metal- and metalloid-containing biomolecules.

title: Metallomics
desc: Metallomics is the integrated study of the metallome — the identity, quantity, distribution, coordination chemistry and biological function of all metals and metalloids in a cell, tissue or organism.

title: Metallophore
desc: A metallophore is a low-molecular-weight molecule secreted by microorganisms to bind and acquire a specific scarce metal ion from the environment or host.

title: Metalloproteome
desc: The metalloproteome is the complete set of metal-binding proteins in an organism or cell, encompassing every protein that requires a metal ion or metal cofactor for its structure or function.

title: Metalloregulation
desc: Metalloregulation is the process by which cells sense intracellular metal-ion concentrations through metal-responsive regulatory proteins that switch target genes on or off to maintain metal homeostasis.

title: Metallostasis
desc: Metallostasis is the coordinated sensing, buffering, trafficking, and sparing of metal ions that keeps each essential metal's bioavailability within a narrow physiological range inside a cell.

title: Mismetallation
desc: Mismetallation is the binding of a metalloprotein's metal site by the wrong metal ion — usually a more competitive one — which inactivates or misdirects the enzyme.

title: Nutritional Immunity
desc: Nutritional immunity is the host defense strategy of controlling transition-metal availability—withholding iron, zinc, and manganese or intoxicating microbes with copper and zinc—to limit the growth of invading pathogens.

title: Siderophore
desc: A siderophore is a small, high-affinity iron(III)-chelating molecule that microbes secrete to scavenge scarce environmental iron and import it into the cell.

title: Stéphane L. Benoit
desc: University of Georgia. Nickel acquisition, hydrogenases, urease, microbial pathogenesis, and nickel chelation.

title: Karen Pendergrass
desc: Karen Pendergrass investigates upstream metal contamination in food systems and agricultural inputs, and how these exposures may influence microbial metabolism and disease. Her work connects exposure pathways with mismetallation and metal-dependent enzyme function, with particular attention to nickel, urease, [NiFe]-hydrogenases, and nickel-dependent forms of glyoxalase I. By examining microbiome and metallomic signatures together, she explores how changes in metal availability and enzyme activity may link microbial communities and heavy-metal exposure to conditions such as endometriosis and Parkinson’s disease. She is the founder of Microbiome Medicine, Heavy Metal Index, Wikibiome, and the Institute of Contaminant Standards (ICS).

title: Divine Aleru
desc: Microbiome research curation, evidence synthesis, disease-associated microbial signatures and medical writing. Microbiome Medicine, Bioconductor, BugSigDB and University of Chester.

title: Nickel & microbes
desc: Ni Urease, [NiFe]-hydrogenases, and nickel-dependent glyoxalase I Nickel supports several specialized microbial enzymes, but using it requires controlled uptake, storage, and delivery to the correct protein. Helicobacter pylori provides a well-studied host-associated example because both urease and hydrogenase require nickel. Other organisms use nickel differently: E. coli glyoxalase I is an instructive case where an enzyme’s metal preference differs from familiar versions in other species. Urease [NiFe]-hydrogenases Glyoxalase I Nickel trafficking H. pylori H. pylori wild type and nickel-storage mutants in mice

title: Strontium & microbes
desc: Sr Urease-linked mineral immobilization Strontium illustrates how microbial activity changes a mineral habitat. Urea-degrading bacteria can drive carbonate precipitation that captures dissolved Sr. The useful process is mineral formation: the element is transferred from water into a solid rather than consumed or destroyed. Urease Biomineralization Carbonate Alkaline-earth metal Environmental microbiology Bacillus sp. TK2d; saline laboratory cultures

title: Titanium & microbes
desc: Ti Nanoparticle exposure and soil nitrogen cycling Titanium connects microbial ecology to both engineered particles and biomaterial surfaces. The clearest distinction is chemical form: titanium dioxide particles dispersed through soil or intestinal contents create different exposures from a fixed metal implant. Soil experiments reveal changes in nitrogen transformations, while gut models show that community composition, population density, metabolism, and spatial organization need separate measurements. A stable diversity index is not a complete test of biological inactivity. Nanoparticles Soil communities Archaea Nitrogen cycle Agricultural-soil microbial community In vitro Human Gut Simulator

title: Copper & microbes
desc: Cu Methane oxidation, copper acquisition, and metal toxicity Copper can be a microbial cofactor, a resource that requires specialized capture, and a stress imposed by the host. Methane-oxidizing bacteria illustrate the acquisition problem; E. coli illustrates damage and defense; macrophage experiments show that host copper transport can influence bacterial survival. The common thread is delivery to a particular molecular target, rather than total copper alone. Methanotrophs Copper trafficking Iron-sulfur damage Culture evidence Metal resistance RAW264.7 macrophages and E. coli

title: Indium & microbes
desc: In Bioleaching electronic waste Acid-producing microbial communities can release indium from discarded displays. They create a leaching environment; the evidence does not imply an indium-dependent metabolism or nutritional requirement. Bioleaching Electronic waste Environmental biotechnology End-of-life LCD panels; acidophilic microbial communities

title: Tungsten & microbes
desc: W Tungstoenzymes and competition with molybdenum Tungsten is a genuine enzyme cofactor in some microbes, including cultured organisms associated with the human gut. Yet tungstate can inhibit other microbes by interfering with molybdenum-dependent metabolism. The direction of an effect therefore depends on the enzyme repertoire, the chemical substrate being processed, and the surrounding ecological conditions. Tungstoenzymes Aldehyde metabolism Molybdenum competition Gut isolates Preclinical evidence B. massiliensis strain phR and its purified oxidoreductase

title: Cesium & microbes
desc: Cs Competition with potassium uptake Cesium uptake can overlap with potassium transport, while resistance may depend on maintaining other intracellular ions. Uptake, tolerance, and useful environmental capture are distinct outcomes. Alkali metal Potassium competition Transport Bioremediation Microbacterium sp. TS-1 and derived mutants

title: Plutonium & microbes
desc: Pu Microbial reduction of oxidized plutonium Microbes can reduce Pu(V/VI) to particle-associated Pu(IV), yet further reduction can produce soluble Pu(III) when suitable ligands are present. Reduction therefore does not invariably immobilize plutonium. Radionuclide Bacterial culture Environmental redox Geobacter metallireducens and Shewanella oneidensis cultures

title: Rhodium & microbes
desc: Rh Antibacterial activity of valproate conjugates Rhodium is being investigated through engineered coordination compounds whose ligands are part of the biological intervention. Two instructive approaches are valproate conjugation and exchangeable nitrogen-donor ligands. Both concern laboratory compound development. Neither demonstrates that exposure to rhodium alone produces the same effect or that a successful bacterial assay predicts a useful treatment. Bacterial culture Coordination chemistry Antimicrobial discovery S. aureus and E. faecium cultures Sensitive and resistant bacterial strains

title: Cerium & microbes
desc: Ce Methanol-dehydrogenase cofactor Cerium has a well-defined role in the methanol-oxidizing machinery of selected bacteria and a separate documented effect on extracellular polymer production. Its biological interpretation depends on chemical form: dissolved Ce(III) in culture is not interchangeable with cerium-oxide nanoparticles or other cerium-containing materials. Lanthanide XoxF Methanol oxidation Methanotrophs Bradyrhizobium sp. MAFF211645

title: Molybdenum & microbes
desc: Mo Molybdenum-cofactor respiration and nitrogen fixation Molybdenum is incorporated into specialized cofactors that enable microbial redox reactions. Respiratory molybdenum cofactors are chemically distinct from the iron–molybdenum cofactor of nitrogenase. In the intestine, their importance depends on available electron donors and acceptors: inflammation can create a metabolic opportunity for organisms able to use these pathways. Molybdenum cofactor Nitrate respiration Enterobacteriaceae Nitrogen fixation Mouse colitis Commensal E. coli in murine colitis models

title: Vanadium & microbes
desc: V Alternative nitrogenase and microbial vanadium reduction Vanadium illustrates two different ways a microbe can use an element: as part of an enzyme that fixes nitrogen, and as an external electron acceptor during anaerobic metabolism. Its importance is conditional. Availability of molybdenum helps determine when alternative nitrogen fixation matters, while vanadium speciation and culture chemistry influence reduction and growth. Alternative nitrogenase Vanadium speciation Environmental microbes Culture evidence Cyanolichens from eastern North American boreal forests

title: Tin & microbes
desc: Sn Organotin transformation and chemical-species dependence Tin–microbe interactions are strongly compound dependent. Environmental bacteria can remove organic groups from tributyltin or add methyl groups to inorganic tin. Separately, organotin exposure can alter a mammalian gut community. Neither process can be generalized to all tin compounds, and transformation does not necessarily reduce toxicity. Organotin Tributyltin Speciation Methylation Environmental microbiology Pure environmental bacterial cultures ICR mice and fecal-community recipients

title: Aluminum & microbes
desc: Al Light-metal exposure and intestinal ecology Aluminum connects environmental microbial adaptation with experimental intestinal ecology. Some bacteria change their metabolism when challenged with aluminum complexes, while oral exposure changes selected gut taxa in mice. These observations describe different biological levels and should be read separately. Aluminum is a light metal; it does not need to be a “heavy metal” to merit attention in metallomics. Gut microbiome Animal studies Light metal Exposure Food- and gut-derived bacterial isolates Pseudomonas fluorescens culture and cell fractions

title: Praseodymium & microbes
desc: Pr Cofactor supporting alcohol oxidation Praseodymium has direct experimental support as a usable metal in bacterial alcohol oxidation. Evidence comes from a nonmethylotrophic soil bacterium and from comparative studies of methylotrophs. This is an element-specific experimental role, rather than an inference based only on the better-known lanthanum and cerium examples. Lanthanide PedH Alcohol dehydrogenase Pseudomonas Pseudomonas putida KT2440 PedH

title: Manganese & microbes
desc: Mn Oxidative-stress defense and environmental manganese cycling Manganese can protect bacterial metabolism from oxidative stress and can also supply energy to specialized environmental communities. At an infection site, access to manganese becomes a contest between microbial defenses and host metal-binding proteins. These functions depend on location and chemical form: manganese in a bacterial enzyme, an abscess, and a mineral-oxidizing culture does not represent the same biological exposure. Superoxide defense Calprotectin Manganese oxidation Environmental microbes Mouse infection S. aureus systemic infection in mice

title: Lanthanum & microbes
desc: La Cofactor in selected bacterial alcohol dehydrogenases Lanthanum is a functional cofactor in selected bacterial alcohol dehydrogenases. Its importance extends beyond fitting a metal into an enzyme: cells must recognize, acquire, transport, and store the ion. The best-characterized systems are specialized environmental bacteria, and their requirements do not imply a lanthanum requirement for people or for every microbiome. Lanthanide ExaF Alcohol dehydrogenase Microbial cofactor Methylobacterium extorquens AM1 and purified ExaF Methylorubrum extorquens AM1 mutants

title: Uranium & microbes
desc: U Respiratory reduction and immobilization Some metal-reducing bacteria conserve energy while converting soluble U(VI) into less soluble U(IV). This respiratory process can immobilize uranium, but its effectiveness depends on the organisms and surrounding geochemistry. Actinide Respiration Uranium reduction Bioremediation Environmental microbiology Uranium-contaminated aquifer; Rifle, Colorado

title: Palladium & microbes
desc: Pd Electron-transfer-driven nanoparticle formation Palladium is a useful example of microbial metal recovery. Bacteria can reduce soluble Pd(II) to elemental Pd(0), forming particles associated with biomass. The reaction links metabolism to materials synthesis, but it does not mean palladium is a nutrient or that every palladium compound behaves alike. Electron transfer Hydrogenase Shewanella Bioreduction Metal recovery Shewanella oneidensis resting cells

title: Magnesium & microbes
desc: Mg Broader metal context: ribosome function and magnesium sensing Magnesium is a major cellular ion that links ribosome stability, energy metabolism, and environmental sensing. Bacteria can monitor magnesium outside the cell through proteins and inside the cell through RNA-based systems. These separate control points help explain why total magnesium is a poor substitute for knowing the available pool at a particular molecular target. Broader metal context Ribosomes PhoPQ Magnesium homeostasis Culture evidence Salmonella, with complementary experiments in E. coli and yeast M-box regulatory RNA

title: Potassium & microbes
desc: K Broader metal context: ion homeostasis and biofilm signaling Potassium is a major intracellular ion whose movement can influence both an individual bacterium and its neighbors. In Bacillus subtilis, uptake is regulated by the second messenger cyclic di-AMP, while channel-mediated potassium release supports coordinated biofilm behavior. These are physiological signaling mechanisms demonstrated in laboratory systems, with their wider ecological prevalence still an open question. Broader metal context Potassium transport Biofilm signaling Cyclic di-AMP Culture evidence B. subtilis laboratory biofilms B. subtilis biofilms and motile P. aeruginosa

title: Germanium & microbes
desc: Ge Strain-dependent tolerance to germanium dioxide Germanium is a metalloid with direct evidence for strain-dependent growth inhibition and ligand-dependent bacterial uptake. The most useful distinction is between tolerating a germanium exposure and accumulating the element: a culture can do one without demonstrating a beneficial biological use for it. Metalloid Bacterial culture Yeast Chemical form Pseudomonas putida ATCC 33015

title: Lithium & microbes
desc: Li RNA sensing and cation export Lithium is a light alkali metal included for its value in understanding bacterial ion sensing and tolerance. The most direct evidence here concerns RNA switches and cation export. These mechanisms help cells respond to an unwanted ion; they do not establish lithium as a broadly required microbial nutrient. RNA sensing Bacterial culture Ion homeostasis Bacterial lithium riboswitches and associated transport genes

title: Tellurium & microbes
desc: Te Tellurite toxicity and reductive resistance Tellurium biology includes both toxicity and specialized respiration. Tellurite, Te(IV), challenges bacterial redox systems, while selected environmental isolates can conserve energy using tellurate, Te(VI). These are distinct chemical species and physiological outcomes; neither should stand in for all tellurium–microbe interactions. Metalloid Tellurite Thiol chemistry Anaerobic metabolism Resistance Bacterial isolates associated with hydrothermal-vent worms

title: Rhenium & microbes
desc: Re Structure-dependent antimicrobial candidates Rhenium compounds show why coordination structure and activation conditions must accompany any antimicrobial claim. Closely related carbonyl complexes can be inactive or active, and illumination can change the bacterial spectrum. The evidence includes chemical screens, computational target hypotheses, and carefully controlled light-versus-dark susceptibility assays. It does not establish an antimicrobial property of elemental rhenium. Bacterial culture Negative result Computational prediction Antimicrobial discovery Eight-microorganism laboratory panel S. aureus cultures and characterized Re(I) complexes

title: Lead & microbes
desc: Pb Oral toxicant and microbiome-dependent bioavailability Lead research now includes experimental microbiota-dependent absorption in mice and observational human studies spanning infancy to later childhood. The evidence supports an interaction between exposure and intestinal ecology, while leaving important causal questions open. Microbial community differences are not a substitute for directly measuring lead exposure. Gut microbiome Bioavailability Animal studies Oral exposure Human WHEALS birth cohort PROGRESS cohort in Mexico City

title: Arsenic & microbes
desc: As Speciation-changing toxicant Arsenic has a two-way relationship with microbial communities: microbes change arsenic chemistry, and arsenic exposure is associated with changes in those communities. Human observations now include longitudinal infant data, while gut simulators and mouse experiments provide more direct tests of transformation and host protection. None of these models alone captures every exposure scenario. Gut microbiome Speciation Methylation Metalloid Human cohort Animal studies Human birth cohort Conventional, germ-free, antibiotic-treated, and genetically modified mice

title: Gadolinium & microbes
desc: Gd Strain-dependent use and bioaccumulation Gadolinium illustrates three different microbial outcomes: use after laboratory adaptation, binding to microbial biomass, and cellular stress in yeast. These should not be conflated. A bacterium able to grow with gadolinium has a particular physiological solution; it does not demonstrate a general nutrient role or a beneficial effect in a host microbiome. Lanthanide Bioaccumulation Adaptation Metal uptake An evolved Methylorubrum extorquens AM1 variant Saccharomyces cerevisiae deletion library

title: Sodium & microbes
desc: Na Broader metal context: sodium gradients, salinity, and gut ecology Sodium belongs to microbial metallomics as an alkali-metal ion with roles in membrane energetics and environmental adaptation. Salt also changes host-associated communities through ecological and host-mediated routes. Sodium gradients, dietary sodium chloride, and circulating microbial metabolites are related but different measurements, and the evidence is clearest when those levels are kept distinct. Broader metal context Sodium bioenergetics Salinity Human pilot Mouse microbiome L. murinus in mice and participants in a small human salt challenge

title: Antimony & microbes
desc: Sb Microbial redox transformations in contaminated environments Antimony is a metalloid involved in microbial oxidation, reduction, and mineral formation. Its environmental fate depends on both the antimony species and the metabolism available in a particular setting. The strongest evidence here comes from isolates, genetic experiments, and sediment studies, rather than human microbiome research. Metalloid Antimonite AnoA Mine sediments Redox Agrobacterium tumefaciens GW4 Anaerobic bacterial isolate MLFW-2

title: Niobium & microbes
desc: Nb Antimicrobial activity versus surface performance Niobium antimicrobial research is strongly formulation-dependent. A niobium oxalate dispersion, niobium pentoxide nanoparticles, and a polymer-bound surface layer are different materials with different opportunities to contact bacteria. The most informative evidence includes an unsuccessful coating experiment: activity against cells in liquid did not automatically prevent a multispecies biofilm from growing on titanium. Biofilm Negative result Bacterial culture Implant materials Defined bacterial cultures and a multispecies flow biofilm E. coli culture

title: Ruthenium & microbes
desc: Ru Experimental antibacterial coordination complexes Ruthenium antibacterial activity belongs to particular coordination compounds and delivery systems. Ligands determine how the metal-containing molecule interacts with cells, while a photosensitizing formulation also depends on illumination. The literature spans resistant Gram-positive isolates, experimental skin infections, and dental biofilms. These are distinct research settings, not interchangeable demonstrations that ruthenium itself is an antibiotic. Coordination chemistry Bacterial culture Antimicrobial discovery S. aureus cultures and a mouse skin-infection model S. mutans–C. albicans on resin

title: Iron & microbes
desc: Fe Iron acquisition, iron-sulfur enzymes, and environmental respiration Iron links nutrient competition, enzyme activity, and environmental respiration. Its oxidation state, ligands, and mineral structure determine what a microbe can use. Host-associated evidence extends from siderophore chemistry to randomized infant-fortification studies, making iron a useful example of why an essential nutrient can produce different microbial outcomes depending on formulation and ecological context. Siderophores Nutritional immunity Iron-sulfur clusters Human intervention Environmental redox Kenyan infants receiving micronutrient powders

title: Selenium & microbes
desc: Se Trace-element nutrition and microbial respiration Selenium is a nonmetal included because microbial cofactor chemistry, environmental respiration, and host nutrient competition intersect. The chemical form and metabolic role are crucial: selenium incorporated into a protein is different from selenate used as a respiratory electron acceptor. Evidence from cultures and mice supports several such roles without establishing a general benefit from increasing selenium exposure. Nonmetal Selenate respiration Gut microbiome Host–microbe competition T. selenatis cultures and nitrate-respiration mutants C. difficile cultures and purified proline reductase

title: Zirconium & microbes
desc: Zr Oral biofilms on zirconia surfaces Zirconium enters this literature mainly as zirconia, the solid zirconium oxide ceramic used in dental components. Its microbial relevance concerns colonization of a surface, not an established nutritional role or the antibacterial action of dissolved zirconium. Studies comparing zirconia with titanium have produced different adhesion results. Surface preparation, organism, time, and the endpoint being measured help explain why a single material ranking is inadequate. Human oral study Biofilm Dental materials Human oral biofilms in 12 volunteers S. sanguinis and S. epidermidis cultures

title: Bismuth & microbes
desc: Bi Antimicrobial metal substitution Bismuth links antimicrobial metallomics to direct metal substitution and broader metabolic disruption. The clearest molecular example is displacement of zinc from bacterial metallo-β-lactamases. Work in Helicobacter pylori, however, shows that bismuth drugs can affect many proteins and pathways. A single substituted metal site is therefore not a universal explanation for every bismuth-sensitive bacterium. Mismetallation Zinc displacement Metallo-β-lactamase Antimicrobial Preclinical Purified MBL enzymes, MBL-positive bacteria, and mice H. pylori exposed to a bismuth drug

title: Osmium & microbes
desc: Os Ligand-dependent bacteriostasis Osmium antimicrobial research spans growth-inhibitory organometallic complexes and a light-activated composite material. These interventions differ in ligand structure, delivery, and mechanism. The most useful evidence combines positive bacterial findings with explicit mammalian-cell comparisons: high potency alone does not establish a clinically useful therapeutic margin. Bacterial culture Antimicrobial discovery Coordination chemistry M. tuberculosis and normal human MRC5 lung cells S. aureus, E. coli, and an infected mouse wound model

title: Mercury & microbes
desc: Hg Microbial methylation and demethylation Mercury illustrates how microbes can both create and transform an exposure hazard. Environmental methylation produces methylmercury, whereas intestinal demethylation can contribute to elimination after ingestion. These reactions occur in different organisms and settings and should not be collapsed into one “mercury detox” pathway. Gut microbiome Methylmercury hgcAB Human study Environmental cycling Two anaerobic bacterial species Public environmental and host-associated metagenomes

title: Cobalt & microbes
desc: Co Corrinoid sharing, vitamin B12 uptake, and metal interference Cobalt sits at the center of vitamin B12 and related corrinoid cofactors, but the surrounding molecule determines who can use it. Microbial communities exchange, compete for, and chemically remodel these cofactors. This molecular ecology is distinct from exposure to free cobalt ions, which can interfere with essential cellular machinery. Cobalamin Corrinoids Nutrient competition Iron-sulfur assembly Gnotobiotic mice B. thetaiotaomicron strains differing in corrinoid transporters A. muciniphila MucT and heterologous E. coli

title: Thorium & microbes
desc: Th Cell-associated sequestration Thorium can be sequestered by bacterial biomass and can alter biofilm communities. These are separate chemical and ecological findings. Actinide Biosorption Phosphate minerals Radionuclide Environmental microbiology River-derived periphytic biofilms in laboratory channels

title: Technetium & microbes
desc: Tc Direct and indirect radionuclide reduction Technetium connects microbial electron transfer to radionuclide mobility. Dissolved Tc(VII), commonly studied as pertechnetate, can be reduced to less soluble Tc(IV). Microbes may catalyze that change directly or generate iron minerals that do the reducing chemistry outside the cell. Radionuclide Environmental redox Biogenic minerals Oak Ridge aquifer sediment microcosms

title: Neodymium & microbes
desc: Nd Structurally verified microbial enzyme cofactor Neodymium connects enzyme structure, metal preference, and mineral acquisition in microbial metallomics. It has been directly identified in an active methanol dehydrogenase, yet not every lanthanide-using bacterium prefers it. Work comparing soluble and poorly soluble neodymium sources also reveals how microbes obtain the metal before using it. Lanthanide XoxF Methanol oxidation Metal selectivity Methylacidimicrobium thermophilum AP8 Methylobacterium extorquens AM1

title: Chromium & microbes
desc: Cr Oxidation-state-dependent stress and reduction Chromium is a case study in why both oxidation state and reaction mechanism matter. Bacteria can help convert chromate, Cr(VI), to Cr(III), but the products may remain soluble. A culture that reduces chromium is not necessarily removing it, and a protein associated with reduction is not automatically a dedicated chromate-reducing enzyme. Chromate Redox Speciation Gut microbiome Animal studies Purified NfoR from Staphylococcus aureus Escherichia coli Fre–flavin biochemical system

title: Thallium & microbes
desc: Tl Experimental intestinal and soil-community stress Thallium has three distinct microbial evidence streams: controlled intestinal exposure in mice, community surveys of contaminated soils, and experiments demonstrating microbial oxidation in freshwater. Together they show why thallium concentration alone is insufficient: chemical species, habitat, and biological activity change the interpretation. Gut microbiome Animal studies Mine soils Exposure Metabolomics C57BL/6J mice Natural freshwater plankton assemblages

title: Barium & microbes
desc: Ba Symbiont-associated biomineralization Marine bacteria and extracellular polymers can concentrate barium and promote barite formation. A sponge symbiont also mineralizes barium internally, demonstrating a distinct host-associated route. Symbiosis Sponge microbiome Biomineralization Alkaline-earth metal Bacterial biofilms in controlled mineralization experiments

title: Gallium & microbes
desc: Ga Iron mimic under antimicrobial investigation Gallium is a test of microbial metal recognition: a metal sufficiently similar to ferric iron can enter iron-handling pathways yet fail to perform the same biochemical work. Research has progressed from Pseudomonas cultures and mouse infections to human trials. That progression matters, because a plausible nutrient-targeting mechanism and an early clinical signal did not guarantee success on a later randomized trial endpoint. Iron mimic Antimicrobial Pseudomonas Biofilm Early clinical research P. aeruginosa cultures and mouse lung infection models Adults with cystic fibrosis and chronic P. aeruginosa infection

title: Platinum & microbes
desc: Pt Microbial reduction of metal complexes Platinum profiles need to separate microbial reduction, resistance, and engineered recovery. Fungi and bacteria can convert soluble platinum species into particles, while resistant cells can alter their physiology under exposure. None of these observations makes platinum an ordinary microbial cofactor. Electron transfer Hydrogenase Bioreduction Nanoparticles Environmental technology Hydrogenase-displaying yeast; anaerobic laboratory system

title: Cadmium & microbes
desc: Cd Toxicant with a specialized algal enzyme exception Cadmium spans two very different biological settings: an experimental intestinal toxicant and a functional enzyme metal in certain marine diatoms. The diatom exception is important for environmental biochemistry, but it is not evidence that cadmium is a human nutrient. Its effects depend on the organism, chemical availability, and the supply of competing metals such as zinc. Gut microbiome Carbonic anhydrase Diatoms Animal studies Metal substitution Marine diatom Thalassiosira weissflogii Zinc-limited diatom cultures

title: Silver & microbes
desc: Ag Antimicrobial ion and resistance pressure Silver illustrates both the power and the ambiguity of metal-based antimicrobial claims. Dissolved Ag(I), metallic particles, their coatings, and the ions released during an experiment are different parts of an exposure. Mechanistic work supports multiple bacterial targets, but particle chemistry and bacterial adaptation can substantially change the outcome. Killing a pathogen in a model does not establish selective benefit to a human microbial community. Antimicrobial Iron homeostasis Biofilms Preclinical E. coli cultures Repeatedly exposed E. coli and P. aeruginosa cultures

title: Neptunium & microbes
desc: Np Coupled microbial reduction and precipitation Microbial Np(V) reduction and removal from water are distinct achievements. Mineral partners and phosphate chemistry influence whether reduced neptunium becomes effectively immobilized. Radionuclide Bioprecipitation Environmental biotechnology Nuclear-legacy sediment microcosms

title: Tantalum & microbes
desc: Ta Host cells, bacteria, and implant surfaces Tantalum highlights a distinction between killing bacteria directly and helping a host resist infection at an implant interface. Two preclinical studies reported favorable infection outcomes despite little or no intrinsic antibacterial advantage in isolated culture assays. Their proposed explanations involve host cells and local immunity, making the living tissue environment part of the material’s effect. Animal model Host–material interface Biofilm S. aureus and S. epidermidis on implant-component pieces Titanium substrates carrying tantalum nanofilms

title: Beryllium & microbes
desc: Be Evidence from bacterial-enzyme inhibition Beryllium has two distinct connections to microbial biochemistry: inhibition of selected enzymes and experimental stabilization of bacterial signaling proteins. These are useful molecular observations, but neither establishes a nutritional role or a characteristic response of an intact microbiome. Beryllium is a light alkaline-earth metal; chemical identity matters more here than the loose label “heavy metal.” Enzyme inhibition Alkaline phosphatase Light metal Evidence gaps Bacterial response-regulator proteins

title: Calcium & microbes
desc: Ca Biofilm architecture, biomineralization, and calcium-responsive signaling Calcium can shape microbial communities as a mineral-building component, a matrix-associated ion, and an environmental signal. Bacillus subtilis and Pseudomonas aeruginosa illustrate different mechanisms. These roles place calcium in broader microbial metallomics, although it is an alkaline-earth metal rather than a heavy metal in conventional usage. Broader metal context Biofilms Calcium carbonate Biomineralization Culture evidence B. subtilis laboratory biofilms P. aeruginosa and clinical airway isolates

title: Other lanthanides & microbes
desc: Ln Comparative enzyme chemistry and evidence gaps Samarium, europium, terbium, dysprosium, holmium, erbium, thulium, ytterbium, and lutetium belong in the atlas, but their evidence is uneven. Comparative enzyme assays cover the series; europium also has direct structural and growth evidence, and samarium has experimental biomineralization evidence. No single “rare-earth effect” should be assigned to every member. Lanthanides Samarium Europium Terbium Dysprosium Holmium Erbium Thulium Ytterbium Lutetium Evidence gaps Methylacidiphilum fumariolicum SolV Yeast and two bacterial species Samarium Sm Europium Eu Terbium Tb Dysprosium Dy Holmium Ho Erbium Er Thulium Tm Ytterbium Yb Lutetium Lu

title: Iridium & microbes
desc: Ir Experimental targeting of biofilm DNA Iridium complexes are being developed for several distinct antibacterial strategies, including extracellular-DNA disruption, light-driven oxidation, and direct growth inhibition. Their ligands and physical conditions define the intervention. A biofilm-active compound, an imaging photosensitizer, and an anti-staphylococcal diamine complex cannot be treated as interchangeable evidence about iridium. Animal model Biofilm Extracellular DNA Antimicrobial discovery Gram-positive biofilms and mouse S. aureus wound infection Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacterial cultures

title: Hafnium & microbes
desc: Hf Surface architecture and bacterial attachment Hafnium research provides two very different antimicrobial examples: nanostructured oxide-coated surfaces and functionalized oxide nanoparticles. In the first, surface geometry is central; in the second, a targeting and polymeric formulation changes interaction with dental bacteria. Neither example supports treating bulk hafnium, dissolved ions, and engineered particles as interchangeable agents. Surface topography Bacterial culture Implant materials S. aureus and E. coli on coated substrates S. mutans biofilms, extracted teeth, and rodents

title: Gold & microbes
desc: Au Detoxification through biomineralization Gold is biologically active when encountered as soluble complexes, even though bulk metallic gold appears inert. Gold-associated bacteria can convert those complexes into less accessible forms. Their chemistry connects detoxification, extracellular molecules, and the formation of elemental gold. Biomineralization Delftibactin Metallophore Environmental microbiology Delftia acidovorans; biochemical and microbial experiments

title: Zinc & microbes
desc: Zn Nutrient limitation, metal competition, and colonization resistance Zinc can support microbial growth, restrict it through competition with another metal, or be withheld by host defenses. Whether zinc favors a pathogen depends on the organism’s uptake systems and the surrounding community. Experiments in pneumococci, Salmonella, and mouse Clostridioides difficile infection demonstrate different mechanisms that should not be collapsed into a single beneficial-or-harmful label. Metal competition Manganese uptake Nutritional immunity Mouse microbiome C. difficile S. Typhimurium during murine intestinal inflammation Mouse microbiota and C. difficile infection

title: Scandium & microbes
desc: Sc Modulation of bacterial gene expression Scandium can alter bacterial gene expression and the production of extracellular enzymes and secondary metabolites. It is a rare-earth element, but not a lanthanide. The evidence here concerns a culture condition that changes microbial behavior, rather than an established scandium-containing enzyme or a universal nutritional requirement. Rare earth Secondary metabolism Gene expression Bacterial culture Streptomyces coelicolor A3(2)

title: Rubidium & microbes
desc: Rb Transport through potassium-handling systems Rubidium is useful for understanding how bacteria distinguish chemically similar alkali-metal ions. It can enter through potassium-handling systems and can partly substitute for potassium under some culture conditions. Transportability, however, is not the same as physiological equivalence: the transporter, strain, and potassium background change the result. Alkali metal Potassium transport Ion selectivity Bacterial culture E. coli potassium transport systems

title: Americium & microbes
desc: Am Microbial accumulation and biosorption Americium research in microbes is mainly about binding and partitioning rather than a demonstrated biological redox cycle. Bacteria, fungal biomass, and dissolved microbial products can change how americium distributes between water, cells, and mineral surfaces. Actinide Radionuclide Biosorption Fungal biomass Environmental microbiology Immobilized Rhizopus arrihizus; laboratory solutions

title: Yttrium & microbes
desc: Y Binding to microbial biomass Yttrium has direct microbial evidence for biosorption and for recognition by a selective metal-binding protein. Neither observation establishes that bacteria require yttrium for growth. Although grouped with the rare-earth elements, yttrium is not a lanthanide, and its biology should be evaluated on its own evidence. Rare earth Biosorption Wastewater Metal recovery Serratia marcescens biomass
